commentary.bottom_line: Five studies test end-user or community involvement in AI design, and all report favorable findings, but none compares a co-designed tool with one built without such input, and samples are small (8 to 33 participants in the evaluated steps). The evidence suggests that participatory design is feasible and acceptable to participants, while its effect on patient outcomes, safety, or equity remains untested.

perspectives.view: The one study labeled an RCT reports its design-related findings as a pre-post analysis and an 8-user pilot. The other four are qualitative or uncontrolled pilots. None has a comparator, outcomes are intermediate (comprehension, acceptability, stakeholder approval), and samples are small. Risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision each lower certainty to very low.

Co-design took several forms, including community-informed chatbot changes, nurse input on camera monitoring, a design sprint, and focus groups with engagement studios. Among 10 pilot users of one co-developed chatbot, 100% used it and 80% scored above 4 on acceptability. One study ended at a simulated prototype and another at an implementation plan, so routine workflow uptake remains largely unmeasured.

A focus group of 19 clinicians, developers, administrators, and patient advocates named limited patient involvement as a challenge, which shows the gap exists. No study testing co-design measured errors, adverse events, or harm. Whether participatory input catches unsafe design choices before deployment is therefore unknown.

After community-informed adaptations, one chatbot's health literacy demands fell 66.7% (12 of 18 items), and all 8 pilot users reported better comprehension. That study enrolled rural, older, minority, limited English proficiency, and low health literacy participants in China. Its small pilot and non-US setting may limit transfer to US Medicaid and safety-net patients.

None of the five studies reports the cost, staff time, or duration of co-design activities. One study recruited 17 adolescents and young adults plus families and clinicians, and another held a 12-provider focus group and community studios with 21 patients. Planners have no published basis for estimating resource needs at scale.

Patients in community engagement studios reported positively about being engaged, and their input shaped algorithm development and a pilot plan. Patient advocates in a separate focus group described limited patient involvement in AI decisions. No study examined whether involvement changed patients' trust in the deployed tool or their access to a human.

Endorsements come from voluntary frameworks such as the CHAI guide and the FUTURE-AI consensus, which state that representative end users should take part in design. The supplied sources cite no binding federal or state requirement for participatory design, and no study examined regulatory compliance outcomes.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI tools designed with and without end-user or disadvantaged-group input on clinical outcomes, safety events, uptake, or performance gaps across subgroups. Studies also do not report the cost and staff time that co-design requires.
commentary.underserved_note: One test, a small pilot in China, included limited English proficiency, low health literacy, rural, older, and minority participants and found lower literacy demands and better reported comprehension. No test reported including Medicaid or US safety-net populations, so benefits for those groups remain inferred rather than shown.
